abstract: A glimpse lasting only a few milliseconds can convey meaningful information about a face, but how the brain transforms such minimal input into stable representations of facial expression and conscious experience remains unclear. Across two experiments using ultra-brief face presentations, we combined hierarchical psychophysical modelling, multivariate EEG decoding, and information-theoretic measures to characterise this transformation. Extending previously reported findings, hierarchical modelling quantified distinct exposure-dependent trajectories for intact-face localisation and expression identification, providing a behavioural calibration of weak, intermediate, and stronger perceptual evidence. The critical neural transition occurred between 4.4 and 6.2 ms. At 4.4 ms, expression sensitivity was behaviourally detectable, but neural expression patterns did not reliably generalise to faces excluded from classifier training. At 6.2 ms, previously observed emotion-related ERP differences were accompanied by expression representations that generalised across faces and locally detectable emotion information during the early posterior negativity (EPN) interval. Subjective clarity tracked location-related neural evidence more consistently than expression-specific evidence, indicating that awareness did not simply mirror the emerging expression representation. The degree to which early centroparietal activity statistically predicted later occipital activity differed between emotional and neutral faces as exposure increased, indicating that the relationship between successive neural responses was reorganised. Thus, a few additional milliseconds of visual input did not merely strengthen facial-expression processing; they transformed weak evidence that did not reliably generalise across faces into more stable, generalisable, behaviourally relevant, and distributed neural information.
